html:
The Theatre of Epidaurus is a stone theatre in the northeast Peloponnese, built in the late 4th century BCE at the edge of the sanctuary of Asclepius. It is often called the most perfect ancient Greek theatre, for its shape and above all its sound.

It is set into a hillside, with rows of limestone seats curving around a full circle for the chorus, the orchestra. An upper tier added in the 2nd century BCE brought the seating to about 13,000 to 14,000. The ancient travel writer Pausanias said it was designed by Polykleitos the Younger. Its acoustics are famous: a word spoken at the centre can be heard in the top row. A study in 2007 suggested that the ridged rows of seats filter out low background noise.

Theatre began in Greece as part of religious festivals (first tragedy at the Dionysia), and here plays and music were part of the healing cult. The theatre is still used. Since 1955 a summer festival has staged the tragedies of Sophocles, Euripides and others in it.
